name: Sustainability
answer: These measures show the carbon, water and energy sourcing behind a data center's operation. AI demand has made data centers one of the fastest growing users of electricity, so these figures are where climate commitments meet actual consumption.

metrics.line: Liters of water consumed by the facility, chiefly for evaporative cooling, per kilowatt-hour of IT energy delivered.
metrics.label: WUE, Water Usage Effectiveness

metrics.line: Kilograms of carbon dioxide emitted, from the grid mix and on-site generation, per kilowatt-hour of IT energy.
metrics.label: CUE, Carbon Usage Effectiveness

metrics.line: The share of facility consumption matched by renewable generation, reported either as annual matching through purchased certificates or as around-the-clock hourly matching.
metrics.label: Renewable energy utilization

reading.body:
Sustainability reporting for data centers reduces to three ratios: water per kilowatt-hour of IT energy, carbon per kilowatt-hour of IT energy, and the share of consumption matched by renewables. Each is measured against delivered IT energy, not total facility draw, so the denominator is the work the building does rather than the power it pulls off the grid.

The pattern is that all three metrics are intensity measures. They describe how cleanly a kilowatt-hour is produced and cooled, not how many kilowatt-hours are consumed. A facility can improve every one of these numbers while its total electricity use, total water withdrawal, and total emissions rise, because AI demand is growing faster than efficiency gains. That distinction matters for AI specifically: the sector's climate exposure is an absolute problem being reported through relative figures.

The renewable metric carries its own ambiguity. Annual matching through purchased certificates and hourly around-the-clock matching are both counted as renewable utilization, and they are not equivalent claims about what actually served the load. A high share under the annual method can coexist with fossil generation running the facility at night.

What this data does not cover: no facility-level values, no targets, no baselines, no time series. It defines the measures and nothing more, so it cannot tell you whether any particular data center is improving, and it cannot be used to compare operators.
